items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we will learn how to compare rational numbers, including:

Content:
- positive and negative fractions, and
- positive and negative decimals.

Content:
This lesson builds directly on ideas we already know. Just like before:

Content:
- numbers to the left on a number line are smaller, and
- numbers to the right on a number line are greater.

Content:
This rule works for all rational numbers, not just integers.

Content:
For example, let’s compare [MATH: \dfrac{4}{7}] and [MATH: -6.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/731285426e640865957af8a1b19c018d]

Content:
First, we plot both numbers on a number line (not to scale):

Content:
- the negative integer, [MATH: -6,] goes to the left of zero, and
- the positive fraction, [MATH: \dfrac{4}{7},] goes to the right of zero.

Content:
Any number to the right is greater than a number to the left, so [MATH: \dfrac{4}{7}] is greater than [MATH: -6.]

Content:
Therefore, the correct statement must be the following:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{4}{7} > -6]

Content:
Let's see more examples.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We cannot compare the fractions directly as they don't have a common denominator.

The least common denominator in this case is [MATH: 36.]

  • To put [MATH: -\dfrac{7}{9}] over a denominator of [MATH: 36,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 4{:}] [MATH: -\dfrac{7}{9} = -\dfrac{7 \times 4}{9 \times 4} = -\dfrac{28}{36}]

  • To put [MATH: -\dfrac{5}{12}] over a denominator of [MATH: 36,] we multiply the numerator and denominator by [MATH: 3{:}] [MATH: -\dfrac{5}{12} = -\dfrac{5 \times 3}{12 \times 3} = -\dfrac{15}{36}]

So, we have two negative fractions, which we write as [MATH: \dfrac{(-28)}{36} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \dfrac{(-15)}{36}.]

Thus, we can now compare the fractions by looking at the numerators only.

Since [MATH: -28 < -15,] the correct statement must be [MATH: -\dfrac{28}{36} < -\dfrac{15}{36},] or, equivalently, [MATH: -\dfrac{7}{9} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{<} -\dfrac{5}{12}.]

sections.normalized_html: The process looks as follows.

sections.normalized_html:
• Step 1: Align the decimal points.

    Always write the decimals so their decimal points line up. If one number has fewer decimal places, you can add trailing zeros without changing its value.

  • Step 2: Remember how negative numbers work.

    When both decimals are negative, they both lie to the left of zero on a number line, and the number closer to zero is greater. To decide which number is closer to zero, we compare their absolute values.

When comparing decimals, we use the same ideas you already know from comparing integers, together with place value and absolute value.

Content:
The process looks as follows.

Content:
- Step 1: Align the decimal points.

Always write the decimals so their decimal points line up. If one number has fewer decimal places, you can add trailing zeros without changing its value.
- Step 2: Remember how negative numbers work.

When both decimals are negative, they both lie to the left of zero on a number line, and the number closer to zero is greater.
To decide which number is closer to zero, we compare their absolute values.

Content:
For example, let’s compare [MATH: -3.14] and [MATH: -0.90.]

Content:
To see which number is closer, we look at their distances from [MATH: 0] using absolute value:

Content:
[MATH: |-3.14| = 3.14
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|-0.90| = 0.90]

Content:
Since [MATH: 0.90 < 3.14,] the number [MATH: -0.90] is closer to [MATH: 0] than [MATH: -3.14.]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: -3.14] is less than [MATH: -0.90,] and the correct comparison is
[MATH: -3.14 < -0.90.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will learn how to compare rational numbers, including:

Content:
- positive and negative fractions, and
- positive and negative decimals.

Content:
This lesson builds directly on ideas we already know. Just like before:

Content:
- numbers to the left on a number line are smaller, and
- numbers to the right on a number line are greater.

Content:
This rule works for all rational numbers, not just integers.

Content:
For example, let’s compare [MATH: \dfrac{4}{7}] and [MATH: -6.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/731285426e640865957af8a1b19c018d]

Content:
First, we plot both numbers on a number line (not to scale):

Content:
- the negative integer, [MATH: -6,] goes to the left of zero, and
- the positive fraction, [MATH: \dfrac{4}{7},] goes to the right of zero.

Content:
Any number to the right is greater than a number to the left, so [MATH: \dfrac{4}{7}] is greater than [MATH: -6.]

Content:
Therefore, the correct statement must be the following:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{4}{7} > -6]

Content:
Let's see more examples.

Item 11 — Tutorial: Comparing Decimals

Content:
When comparing decimals, we use the same ideas you already know from comparing integers, together with place value and absolute value.

Content:
The process looks as follows.

Content:
- Step 1: Align the decimal points.

Always write the decimals so their decimal points line up. If one number has fewer decimal places, you can add trailing zeros without changing its value.
- Step 2: Remember how negative numbers work.

When both decimals are negative, they both lie to the left of zero on a number line, and the number closer to zero is greater.
To decide which number is closer to zero, we compare their absolute values.

Content:
For example, let’s compare [MATH: -3.14] and [MATH: -0.90.]

Content:
To see which number is closer, we look at their distances from [MATH: 0] using absolute value:

Content:
[MATH: |-3.14| = 3.14
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|-0.90| = 0.90]

Content:
Since [MATH: 0.90 < 3.14,] the number [MATH: -0.90] is closer to [MATH: 0] than [MATH: -3.14.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/890de55df56cd7075cb5d01cb6f95826]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: -3.14] is less than [MATH: -0.90,] and the correct comparison is
[MATH: -3.14 < -0.90.]

Both numbers are negative, so they are both to the left of zero on a number line.

Among negative numbers, the one closer to zero is greater.

To see which number is closer, we look at their distances from [MATH: 0] using absolute value:

[MATH: |-3.28| = 3.28
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|-3.6| = 3.6]

Since
[MATH: 3.28 < 3.6,]
the number [MATH: -3.28] is closer to [MATH: 0] than [MATH: -3.6.]

Therefore, [MATH: -3.28] is greater than [MATH: -3.6,] and the correct comparison is the following:

[MATH: -3.28 \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{>} -3.6]
